interactions: Trientine or D-penicillamine with zinc, oral iron or food: chelation reduces absorption; take on an empty stomach and at least 1 hour apart from other oral medicines, zinc and iron.
Lactulose or rifaximin with sertraline, spironolactone or a chelator: no clinically relevant interaction.
output.proposed: Review of trientine or D-penicillamine and zinc with sertraline, spironolactone, lactulose and rifaximin
output.summary: Chelators must be separated from food, zinc, iron and other oral medicines. Sertraline needs a lower dose in cirrhosis. No clinically relevant interaction with lactulose or rifaximin.
warnings: Sertraline in cirrhosis: exposure increases; use a lower or less frequent dose and monitor sodium (SSRI-associated hyponatremia).

Chelation in neurological Wilson disease: early neurological worsening can occur with either agent; start low and escalate slowly. D-penicillamine also causes hypersensitivity, marrow suppression and proteinuria.
Spironolactone: monitor potassium and creatinine during lactulose titration.
Avoid antipsychotics (extrapyramidal worsening), benzodiazepines and opioids.

action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies precipitants; cirrhosis with Kayser-Fleischer rings and a movement disorder requires copper studies.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not give haloperidol or other antipsychotics for agitation: they can markedly worsen the dystonia and parkinsonism of neurological Wilson disease.
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not accept the 'cryptogenic cirrhosis' and 'essential tremor' labels: the Wilson diagnosis changes treatment and family screening.
Do not give copper-containing supplements or trace-element mixtures with copper.
required_recommendations: Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Add rifaximin 550 mg twice daily to lactulose to prevent recurrence, since this episode occurred on lactulose prophylaxis (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Identify and treat the precipitant: no infection, bleeding or electrolyte disturbance was found; the cause is progressive liver disease from untreated Wilson disease, so chelation treats it.

Start chelation with trientine (or D-penicillamine) at a low dose escalated slowly, with hepatology and neurology input, watching for early neurological worsening; zinc for maintenance after the initial phase (AASLD Wilson 2022).

Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 18 (EASL 2018); the decision weighs the response of liver function to chelation (AASLD Wilson 2022).
Educate about a low-copper diet during initial treatment (avoid shellfish, liver, mushrooms, nuts, chocolate).
Screen first-degree relatives, starting with the sibling with early liver disease and the children: liver tests, ceruloplasmin, slit-lamp examination and targeted testing for the two ATP7B variants.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.

accepted: Acute hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II) superimposed on previously unrecognized Wilson disease: neurologic features (KF rings, wing-beating tremor, cerebellar ataxia, basal ganglia changes) in 'cryptogenic' cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 18); copper metabolism is the missing diagnosis.

differential.key_features: KF rings, wing-beating tremor, dystonia and 'cryptogenic' cirrhosis with ceruloplasmin 8 mg/dL, 24-hour urine copper 284 µg/24h, the MRI deep grey matter and midbrain pattern and two ATP7B variants: Leipzig score above 4.
Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL and TSH 1.9 mIU/L are normal.
Wing-beating tremor + dystonia + ataxia is NOT essential tremor; the original attribution was incorrect.
Antidepressant tremor would not produce dystonia or KF rings.
The copper studies and KF rings explain the liver disease; no feature of autoimmune hepatitis.
Parkinsonism and ataxia with pallidal T1 hyperintensity occur in cirrhosis, but KF rings, low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper and putaminal and midbrain T2 change indicate Wilson disease.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh C (11: bilirubin 3.2 3, albumin 2.8 2, INR 1.7 2, mild ascites 2, HE grade II 2); MELD-Na 18 (creatinine 0.9, bilirubin 3.2, INR 1.7, sodium 136).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Unexplained or 'cryptogenic' liver disease with neurological or psychiatric features requires a Wilson work-up at any age; late presentations after 40 occur (AASLD Wilson 2022).

Leipzig score: KF rings 2, severe neurological symptoms 2, ceruloplasmin below 10 mg/dL 2, 24-hour urine copper more than twice the upper limit 2, a total of 8 before genetics; 4 or more establishes Wilson disease. The two pathogenic ATP7B variants add 4 once they are shown to lie on different chromosomes (phase is not yet determined) (AASLD Wilson 2022).
Wing-beating tremor and KF rings are highly specific for Wilson disease; the prior 'essential tremor' label was a misattribution.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: HE superimposed on unrecognized Wilson disease masquerading as cryptogenic cirrhosis and essential tremor; KF rings, low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper, wing-beating tremor and the basal ganglia and midbrain imaging are the clues; chelation starts low and escalates slowly in neurological Wilson disease.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 3 required actions (core labs with copper studies, diagnostic paracentesis, MRI) + recommended infection screen and ATP7B testing; a rare cause of cirrhosis hidden behind two prior labels; high stakes for the family.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. N. is a 55-year-old man with a 5-year history of 'cryptogenic cirrhosis' and tremor attributed to essential tremor, now presenting with acute worsening of confusion, tremor, and dystonia over 2 weeks. His wife reports he has had mood swings, behavioral changes, and difficulty with word-finding for several months — dismissed as depression and stress. His neurological exam reveals Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp, wing-beating tremor, cerebellar ataxia, and dystonia.

neurological_exam.additional: Mild scleral icterus. Mild ascites. Wing-beating tremor, dystonia, and Kayser-Fleischer rings present on examination.
neurological_exam.coordination: Cerebellar-type dysmetria on finger-nose testing. Truncal ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Kayser-Fleischer rings visible on slit-lamp examination — golden-brown deposits at corneal periphery. Pupils reactive. Extraocular movements intact with mild slowing of saccades. Mild dysarthria.
neurological_exam.gait: Dystonic gait — unsteady with abnormal posturing.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Disoriented to time. Slowed speech. Asterixis mild bilaterally. Wife reports behavioral changes and mood swings for several months.
neurological_exam.motor: Wing-beating tremor bilateral arms. Increased tone (extrapyramidal). No focal weakness.
